title: To Build a Fire
text:
On a gray winter morning in the Yukon, a man set out alone along a frozen creek to join his companions at a mining camp. It was his first winter in the north. It was far colder than he knew: when he spat, the spit crackled in the air before it hit the snow. A big husky dog trotted with him. The dog's instinct told it that this was no time to travel, but it followed.

An old timer at Sulphur Creek had warned the man that no one should travel alone in the Klondike when it was colder than fifty below. The man had laughed at that. He was alert and capable, and he would be in camp by six.

Then he broke through thin ice over a hidden spring and soaked his legs to the knees. He knew what to do: build a fire and dry his feet. He built it under a spruce tree and it caught. But the tree's boughs were heavy with snow, and the heat and his movements shook them. The snow slid down and put the fire out.

His fingers were now numb and useless. He lit all his matches at once, burning his hands, but the second fire failed. He tried to kill the dog to warm his hands in its body and could not hold it. He ran until he collapsed. As he froze, he admitted that the old timer had been right. The dog waited, then went on toward the camp.
lesson: Confidence is no substitute for experience. When someone who has survived the conditions gives you a rule, follow it, especially when it seems overcautious.
people: A man, his dog, the old timer from Sulphur Creek
source: Jack London, To Build a Fire (1908)
